source.title: What is the best model? Application-driven Evaluation for Large Language Models
source.authors: Shi-Guo Lian; Kai-Kai Zhao; Xinhui Liu; Xuejiao Lei; Bikun Yang; Wen-Jing Zhang; Kai Wang; Zhao-Xiang Liu

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether downstream task accuracy improves with model scale, using a zero-shot application benchmark rather than held-out pretraining loss or compute-scaling fits.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws and evaluates accuracy across model scales, but it does not measure cross-entropy loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or compare compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Numerical values are presented in figures but are not included in the supplied text; rows record only outcomes stated in prose.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates eight Qwen1.5-Chat sizes (0.5B–110B) on a new application benchmark and reports how zero-shot accuracy changes with scale. That is a new setting with a result on V6. It fits no curve and makes no prediction, so only the 'improves with scale' part of V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say larger Qwen1.5-Chat models perform better overall, 'aligning with the scaling law'. The size range with the largest gains and the plateau point depend on difficulty. They propose choosing the smallest model that reaches a desired accuracy for the given tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses zero-shot accuracy on an application-oriented benchmark of instruction-tuned chat models, rather than fitting held-out pretraining loss across parameter, token, or compute scales.
record.method_sensitivity: Accuracy levels depend on the scoring threshold; the paper reports lower accuracy at higher thresholds, while scale trends remain consistent across thresholds. The scale range with the greatest gains varies by difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: Small models (0.5B–4B) are sensitive to the difficulty change from easy to medium but not from medium to hard; larger models (14B–110B) show the opposite pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How sensitive downstream accuracy is to item difficulty shifts with model scale.

record.peer_reviewed: Natural Language Processing and Chinese Computing
record.problems: Only one model family is evaluated; the study reports no uncertainty estimates. The supplied text does not include the numerical accuracy values displayed in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 7 presents accuracy by task and sub-task, but the text does not state the individual outcomes; no task-specific rows were extracted. The model-selection example in Figure 8 uses plotted intersections and is not a separate model-performance result.

untested.parts: Whether gains are predictable (no fitted trend, extrapolation or loss-based prediction); dependence on pretraining loss; other model families.
Not tested: no pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested: no fits or extrapolation.
Not tested: only instruction-tuned text models are evaluated, with no power-law fits.

missing.what: Relative percentage accuracy improvement between successive model sizes by difficulty, which quantifies the diminishing returns

record.verdict_notes: One model family; eight sizes. All numbers are figure-only and no uncertainty is reported. The automatic judge (Qwen1.5-72B-Chat) belongs to the evaluated family. The differing training data and tokens across sizes are not discussed. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy and power-law relationships with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures zero-shot benchmark accuracy across model sizes, not a fitted predictive relationship or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
It does not fit exponents or compute-optimal splits, or test how those fits change with setup choices.

rows.subject: Qwen1.5-Chat series
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero-shot accuracy across model sizes for easy questions.
rows.value: Accuracy increases with scale; the greatest increase is from 0.5B to 7B, and improvement diminishes significantly above 7B. Exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The prose reports increasing accuracy as well as a marked reduction in gains beyond 7B.
rows.check: Accuracy rises, but gains diminish significantly beyond 7B. This may reflect a ceiling on easy items, which the study does not separate out.

rows.note: The prose reports increasing accuracy, with the range of greatest improvement and onset of a bottleneck differing from easy questions.
rows.check: Accuracy rises, with a bottleneck at 14B; the same possible ceiling confound as R4.
